pairs.narration: Ask Claude for a deck, and you get a deck.
pairs.note: Narrator's hook. The post's nearest line is in the Altitude section (not quoted here): Claude will happily make you some slides.

pairs.narration: Felix Rieseberg, an engineering manager at Anthropic
pairs.note: EM expanded to engineering manager: faithful.

pairs.narration: would send a short seller after it
pairs.note: Narrator's framing; the post brings in a short seller as part of a red team.

pairs.narration: On his blog, he calls this range drawing on several fields, not just the one the task seems to need.
pairs.post: Drawing on multiple fields rather than just the one the task might need at the surface, using knowledge, tools, and techniques you normally wouldn't.
pairs.note: multiple to several; might need at the surface to seems to need; tail about knowledge, tools and techniques dropped.

pairs.narration: Now that multi-agent setups are easier to run, he's seen really interesting results asking Claude to bring in extra fields.
pairs.post: As AI products make it easier and easier to run multi-agent systems (with multiple threads, orchestrators, or simply subagents), I've seen really interesting results by imploring Claude to bring in additional fields.
pairs.note: Drops the feature detail (threads, orchestrators, subagents) and softens imploring to asking.

pairs.narration: His first trick is an old one from The Art of Innovation by Tom Kelley and Jonathan Littman.
pairs.post: An old trick from The Art of Innovation by Tom Kelley and Jonathan Littman.
pairs.note: Faithful attribution.

pairs.narration: Replace the noun with verbs.
pairs.post: Try to replace the nouns with verbs:
pairs.note: Drops Try to; nouns becomes noun.

pairs.narration: A quarterly review isn't a deck. It's getting busy people to believe a story about cause and effect and to decide under uncertainty in 30 minutes.
pairs.post: A quarterly review isn't "a deck". It's "getting busy people to believe a story about cause and effect, and to decide under uncertainty, in 30 minutes".
pairs.note: Word for word apart from punctuation and quote marks.

pairs.narration: The verbs make it easier for you and Claude to see which fields could add a useful angle.
pairs.post: Having the verbs makes it easier for both me and Claude to understand which fields might bring in a unique and useful perspective.
pairs.note: Paraphrase; me becomes you; unique dropped.

pairs.narration: His second trick is what every heist movie spends its first half hour on.
pairs.post: every single heist movie spends the first 30 minutes assembling a diverse cast of characters and talents.
pairs.note: 30 minutes becomes half hour. In the post the heist line is in the Range intro, not the crew trick.

pairs.narration: Assemble the crew.
pairs.note: Same words.

pairs.narration: Felix pretends the deck has to be amazing, or aliens blow up Earth.
pairs.post: The deck needs to be amazing, otherwise aliens will blow up Earth.
pairs.note: Narrator adds pretends: the post states the stake as a premise.

pairs.narration: For production quality, he'd bring in an analyst, a journalist, and an editor.
pairs.post: For production quality, I'd bring in an analyst, a journalist, and an editor.
pairs.note: Verbatim except I'd becomes he'd.

pairs.narration: If it gets presented, a motion and audio designer, too.
pairs.post: If it has to be presented, probably a motion and audio designer, too.
pairs.note: Drops probably.

pairs.narration: Then a red team to attack it, a short seller, and a forensic accountant.
pairs.post: It might be useful to employ an adversarial "red team", too, so let's bring in a short seller and a forensic accountant.
pairs.note: Meaning shift risk: in the post the short seller and forensic accountant ARE the red team; the narration lists three items. Also might be useful becomes a definite step.

pairs.narration: He admits this takes creativity.
pairs.post: Putting this into practice isn't easy; it requires you to be creative.
pairs.note: Paraphrase.

pairs.narration: Until his colleague Alex Albert used Blender to render interior designs, he'd never thought of using Claude for 3D environments on his homepage. And he's made video games before.
pairs.post: Until I saw my colleague Alex Albert use Blender to render interior designs, I never considered using Claude for 3D environments for my homepage - even though I've previously made video games!
pairs.note: Close; I saw dropped (the post says he saw it, not that Alex used Blender with him).

pairs.narration: His homepage is a 3D room now.
pairs.note: Not in the post. Supported by the homepage HTML (WebGL room, ?room=1) saved in sources/src-felix-homepage.raw.html and On-screen: FELIXRIESEBERG.COM - HOMEPAGE - CAPTURED 2026-10-21 (frame-0084).

pairs.narration: He says this is where he sees the most magic.
pairs.post: However, this is easily where I see the most magic happen.
pairs.note: Close; easily dropped.

pairs.narration: Before your next big ask, write the verbs, then name the crew.
pairs.note: Narrator's call to action, not in the post.

pairs.narration: And have Claude do what a short seller does to research a position, not write like one.
pairs.post: Don't ask the model to write like a short seller, ask it to do what a short seller does to research their position.
pairs.note: Order swapped, model becomes Claude (the post says the advice is not model-specific).

pairs.narration: Role-play makes the transcript weirder, not the result better.
pairs.post: It is easy to accidentally engage in role play, which will make your transcript weirder without improving the actual outcome.
pairs.note: Compressed; meaning kept.

pairs.narration: Who joins your crew first? The short seller or the forensic accountant?
pairs.note: Narrator's engagement question.
